claims.text: Total cost of ownership adds up what an option costs over a stated period: getting it, running it, operating it, changing it and leaving it; every option is counted over the same period.

People's time (building, upgrading, handling failures, learning the tool) is often the largest cost line, so an option with no fee can need the most work. In ADR 0009 time is the largest cost for A and B; for C it is the fee.

Getting and leaving are paid once; operating and a yearly fee repeat each year, so an option quick to get can be dearer over three years. Comparing over the same period and needs matters more than precise numbers.

Named assumptions, with ranges where unsure, let a reader change one (such as the price of a person-day) and see whether the order of the options changes; that assumption is the one worth checking first.

ADR 0009 was written in Sprint 16 for a stage-2 choice; its figures were estimated when the ADR was written, and at decision time the team compared only in words. Options: own code, Keycloak run by the team, a paid sign-in service.

ADR 0009 lines 27-29: every figure is the team's assumption, not a quote; time in person-days of one developer; ranges where unsure; fees in millions of đồng. Lines 33-38: getting, running, fee, operating, changing, leaving rows.
In ADR 0009 option A's running cost is near zero as it runs inside the API (line 34), it has a fee of 0 in every row, and leaving does not apply to it (line 38).

ADR 0009 three-year totals: person-days A 79-145, B 46-91, C 19-44 (line 39); fees A 0, B 30-60 million, C 90-270 million (line 40). C's getting line is 5-8 days; its fee is 30-90 million a year and grows with users.

ADR 0009 main assumptions: three years, under 50,000 customer accounts, one new sign-in feature a year, about 2 million đồng per person-day; converted (person-days x 2 million + 3-year fees, rounded): A about 160-290, B 120-240, C 130-360 million; A and B overlap, B lower at both ends.
ADR 0009 lines 45-47: B and C overlap; changing the number-of-users assumption (C's fee grows with it) or the price of a person-day is enough to swap their order, so the team states both.
A quote prices only the fee; in ADR 0009 the option with no fee, the team's own code, needs the most person-days.
A comparison built on named assumptions and ranges, without any quote, is still useful: it shows which assumptions could change the order, and those are what to check more closely.

The team's time is not free when it has more work than people: a person-day spent on a sign-in component is not spent on the core domain; a team with truly idle time pays less for it. ADR 0009 counts a person-day at about 2 million đồng.

Rebuilt from the table: B = 8-12 + 3x(10-20) + 3x(1-3) + 5-10 = 46-91 person-days. At 1 million đồng per person-day, A is about 79-145 million and B about 76-151 million (adding 30-60 million to run).
ADR 0009's decision section also rejects A because it carries a security risk the team lacks the expertise to handle.
